I’m going to read the policy’s general eligibility section too, because it often adds baseline Medicaid-age/category requirements, and then I’ll check amendments.## General eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 (Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA))**, NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets these **general eligibility criteria**:

1. **Is enrolled in NC Medicaid.**  
   The policy states that an eligible beneficiary must be enrolled in the NC Medicaid program, and notes that a beneficiary’s eligibility category may include service restrictions that make them ineligible for CAP/DA.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 2.1.1 — “General” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

2. **Meets nursing-facility level of care (LOC).**  
   The beneficiary must meet the required **HCBS nursing facility LOC** as determined by NC Medicaid and need long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

3. **Has an assessed need for at least one CAP/DA waiver service.**  
   The completed CAP assessment must show a **reasonable indication** that the person will need a service plan for at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of evaluation.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

4. **Has a signed service plan authorizing waiver services.**  
   The beneficiary must have a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be rendered monthly to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management.  
   The policy also allows coverage where the signed service plan authorizes short-term **equipment, modification, or technology** needed to return to or remain in the primary private residence and avoid institutional placement.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

5. **Can remain safely in the home or approved setting with supports.**  
   The beneficiary must be able to maintain **health, safety, and well-being** in the **primary private residence or an approved location** with both **formal and informal supports**.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

6. **Is cost-effective compared with institutional care.**  
   The person’s **paid care needs** must be maintainable **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

7. **Has a primary physician.**  
   The beneficiary must have a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate all medical services.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

8. **Has an emergency back-up and disaster plan.**  
   The policy requires an emergency back-up/disaster plan identifying who will provide care when direct care staff are unavailable, the primary caregiver has an emergency, or there is a public health emergency.  
   **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Plain-language summary

In plain English, a person generally qualifies for **CAP/DA** if they:

- **have NC Medicaid,**
- **need nursing-facility level care,**
- **can be safely served at home or another approved community setting instead of an institution,**
- **need at least one CAP/DA waiver service,**
- **have an approved signed service plan,**
- **meet the program’s cost-effectiveness requirement,**
- **have a coordinating physician,** and
- **have a backup plan for emergencies.**

## Important limitation

The policy section I retrieved does **not** explicitly say in that section that CAP/DA is limited to adults, even though the title of Policy 3K-2 is **“Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA).”** I did not retrieve a section that states a specific age cutoff verbatim, so I’m not going to infer one beyond the document title alone.

## Priority status is not the same as eligibility

The policy also lists certain groups for **priority consideration**—for example, some people transitioning from CAP/C, nursing facilities, or hospice—but those are **priority categories**, not the core eligibility criteria themselves.  
**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.4 — “Priority Consideration for CAP/DA Participation” (effective 2025-09-01) [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Current policy version

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 — “Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)” [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 5B (Orthotics & Prosthetics)**, the policy specifically says the following are **not covered**:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience** or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** to keep at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in the policy’s care-coordination section

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For an orthotic or prosthetic item to be covered, the policy requires both the **general Medicaid coverage criteria** and the **orthotics/prosthetics-specific criteria**.

### 1) General Medicaid coverage criteria
The item or service must be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- Able to be **safely furnished**
- Not replaceable by an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**
- Furnished in a way **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 3.1 — “General Criteria Covered”**: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### 2) Orthotics/prosthetics-specific coverage criteria
The policy also says orthotics or prosthetics are covered only if:

- They are **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- They are **medically necessary to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level**
- They are **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting in which normal life activities take place**
- There was a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering physician, PA, or NP related to the primary reason the beneficiary needs the orthotic/prosthetic, **no more than 6 months before** initiation
- The beneficiary’s need is **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician, PA, or NP

The policy further states:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a **replacement for all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary must need the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes**

In addition, orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:

- A **reasonable and medically necessary part** of the treatment plan
- **Consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms
- Of **high quality**, with **replacement parts available and obtainable**

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”**: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Other general noncoverage rules
The policy also says the service is not covered if:

- The beneficiary does **not meet the eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0
- The beneficiary does **not meet the criteria** in Section 3.0
- The procedure, product, or service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service
- The procedure, product, or service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Section 4.1 — “General Criteria Not Covered”**: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

per_question.agent_answer:

Next I’m pulling that discharge section and checking whether Policy 8C has been amended so I can give you the current rule.Here are the **current NC Medicaid criteria** for **outpatient behavioral health services** under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C** (effective **April 15, 2025**): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 1. Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets the **entrance criteria** if the policy’s listed requirements are met, including:

- A **current DSM-5 diagnosis** (or subsequent edition);
- The beneficiary presents **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with the diagnosis;
- If a **higher level of care is indicated but unavailable**, or the beneficiary is **refusing that higher level of care**, outpatient services can be provided **until the appropriate level of care is available** or to **support the beneficiary to participate** in that higher level of care;
- The beneficiary is **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on North Carolina community practice standards.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.1 — “Entrance Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 2. Continued service criteria
For **continued services**, the policy requires:

### First, any **one** of the following:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; **or**
- There is a **tenuous nature of the functional gains**.

### And, in addition, any **one** of the following:
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, and **additional goals are indicated** as evidenced by documented symptoms; **or**
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals** and there is documentation supporting that.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.2 — “Continued Service Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 3. Discharge criteria
The policy states discharge is appropriate when **any** of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive** the services; **or**
- Based on the beneficiary’s presentation and **failure to show improvement despite modifications in the treatment plan**, the beneficiary requires a **more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.3 — “Discharge Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 4. Scope note
Policy 8C applies only if the person is an **eligible NC Medicaid beneficiary**, and the provider must verify eligibility each time services are rendered. The beneficiary may also have **service restrictions tied to eligibility category** that make them ineligible for this service.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 2.1.1 — “General” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## 5. Amendment status
I checked amendments for Policy 8C. The authoritative current document is **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, effective April 15, 2025**. I did not find a separate change notice amending it in the database.

## Plain-language summary
In short, NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services are for beneficiaries who:

- Have a **current mental health diagnosis**,
- Have symptoms and functional impairment tied to that diagnosis,
- Can **benefit from outpatient treatment**, and
- Do not have a more effective alternative intervention identified.

Services may continue when the person still needs treatment, remains at risk of relapse, or has fragile gains, **and** is either progressing or has new documented goals. Discharge happens when the person has improved enough, wants to stop, or needs a different treatment approach because outpatient care is not working.

For **outpatient specialized therapies** under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, the **EPSDT special provision** means a Medicaid beneficiary **under age 21** may receive services beyond ordinary policy limitations **when the service is medically necessary under EPSDT**. The policy’s EPSDT section states that EPSDT is an **“Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age”** and cites **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r)**. The same section also makes clear EPSDT does **not** require coverage of a service that is:

- **unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational**, or
- **not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment**.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 2.2.1 — “EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age” (effective 2025-02-01). For children, the policy indicates therapy is governed by **medical necessity** rather than the adult annual visit caps. In the under-21 visit-guidelines section, the policy says:

- **Speech-language and audiology therapy services are limited to the need for services based upon the severity of the deficit**;
- services are limited to the **number of medically necessary visits within an authorization period**; and
- **an authorization period cannot exceed six calendar months**.

That section gives severity-based ranges for speech-language/audiology therapy:
- **Mild impairment:** **6 to 26** visits
- **Moderate impairment:** **up to 46** visits
- **Severe impairment:** **up to 52** visits

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 5.4 — “Medical Necessity Visit Guidelines for Beneficiaries Under 21 Years of Age,” especially Section 5.4.2 — “Speech-Language-Audiology Therapy” (effective 2025-02-01). [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

By contrast, the policy separately has a section titled **“Visit Limitations Beneficiaries 21 Years of Age and Older,”** which indicates the adult limits are treated differently. So the basic effect of EPSDT here is: **children under 21 are not confined to the same adult-style policy limitations when additional medically necessary therapy is needed**, so long as the service still satisfies Medicaid coverage standards and is not unsafe/experimental/non-medical.

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A identifies the following as authorized **ordering practitioners** for outpatient therapy services:

- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**

The policy section I retrieved does **not** state a different ordering-practitioner list specifically for beneficiaries under 21; based on the text retrieved, this is the list that applies in the policy.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section 3.1.2 — “Ordering Practitioners” (effective 2025-02-01). [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A also expressly says that if the therapy service **requires prior approval**, being under 21 **does not eliminate that requirement**:

- “**If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.**”

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, subsection titled “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements” (effective 2025-02-01). [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

- **EPSDT can broaden coverage** for outpatient therapy services for Medicaid beneficiaries **under 21** when the therapy is **medically necessary**.

- services by other licensed health care professionals,
- respite care,
- transportation,
- financial management,
- errands,
- companion sitting or leisure activities,
- ongoing supervision/monitoring,
- tasks not identified in the assessment and service plan, and

## Short answer

A CAP/DA beneficiary **can transfer** when moving to a different county, and the **CME** (case management entity) must coordinate the transfer so there are **no gaps in service provision**. The policy also includes transition rules for a **CAP/C beneficiary aging into CAP/DA**.

## Rules that govern transfers

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3 — “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries”** (effective **2025-09-01**) ([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)):

### General transfer requirements
Before a transfer occurs, the CME must:

- **determine the anticipated start date of service;**
- **coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;**
- **discuss and plan for the health, safety, and well-being of the beneficiary;**
- **initiate transfer of the electronic health records in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;**
- **arrange for a home visit within five business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, by the receiving entity, to assess the home environment and identify health/welfare concerns and needed mitigation/safety planning; and
- **coordinate and plan for services to start on the first date of the transfer.**

That means the governing rule is not just “yes, transfer is allowed,” but also that the transfer must be **actively coordinated** to maintain continuity of care.

### If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county
The same section specifically says that for a **CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to a different county**:

- the **transferring CME** must coordinate the transfer with the **receiving CME** on the agreed transfer date, or **within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- the transferring and receiving agencies must **discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being**;
- the **electronic health record must be transferred** to the receiving county;
- the **receiving CME must arrange a home visit within five business days** after the move to the new primary residence; and
- the CME must **coordinate services to begin on the first date of transfer into the receiving county**.

## CAP/C to CAP/DA transition rule
The same section also governs a separate kind of transfer: a **CAP/C beneficiary aging out of CAP/C and moving into CAP/DA**. In that situation, Section 3.3 requires:

- a **transition/transfer plan 12 months prior to the birth month**;
- completion of a **transition plan during the annual needs review assessment at age 20**;
- consultation with the beneficiary and primary caregiver about **other Medicaid and community resources** after age 21;
- a **multidisciplinary team meeting 90 calendar days prior** to the birth month or transfer month;
- notice to the **local DSS in the month prior** so the CAP evidence code can be changed; and
- **CAP/DA services to be authorized and provided on the first day** of the birth month or identified transfer month.

## Provider-side rule relevant to transfers
A transfer also depends on provider participation requirements. Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 6.5 — “Medicaid Provider Requirement to Provide CAP/DA Waiver Services”** (effective **2025-09-01**) ([Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)), CAP/DA providers must, among other things:

- **register as a user of e-CAP and participate in required trainings;**
- **accept, decline, or acknowledge service authorizations within three business days** in e-CAP;
- complete CAP/DA orientation and annual updates;
- attest to required policies on restraints/seclusion and incident management; and
- attest to background-check compliance.

So, as a practical matter, transfers are governed by both:
1. the **beneficiary transfer procedures** in **Section 3.3**, and
2. the **provider participation/authorization requirements** in **Section 6.5**.

## Bottom line
**Yes, a CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer between service providers/counties, but the transfer must be coordinated by the CME under Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3.** The policy requires a transition plan, coordination between the old and new agencies, transfer of the electronic record, a home visit within five business days after the move, and services to begin on the first day of transfer so there is no gap in care.

- **The assurances required by 42 CFR 441.302** and the **supporting documentation required by 42 CFR 441.303**.
- Any applicable requests to waive Medicaid requirements concerning:
  - **statewide application**,
  - **comparability of services**, and
  - **income/resource rules for medically needy individuals living in the community**.

  - **only to beneficiaries who are not inpatients** of a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, and
  - **only to beneficiaries who, absent waiver services, would require Medicaid-covered institutional level of care** in a hospital, NF, or ICF/IID.

- **Health and welfare** protections for beneficiaries;
- **Provider standards**, including compliance with state licensure/certification requirements where applicable;
- Compliance of certain facilities with applicable standards;

- be **age 18 or older**,
- be **aged 65+** or otherwise disabled as described there,

## Short answer

An NC Innovations waiver participant may request services that cost more than their individual base budget if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines services are medically necessary, they will be authorized regardless of the base budget. If a request is denied, the participant must be told the reasons and how to appeal, and the policy also says they may file a grievance regarding the base budget if they wish to do so.

## What the policy says

Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P states:

- the participant may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget;
- the results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized, and if the LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget; and
- if any request for authorization of services is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal.

It also says the individual should be told how to file a grievance regarding the base budget if he or she wishes to do so.

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, section titled **Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes** (effective 2016-11-01; current per amendment check): [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## What happens if they think the budget is too low

If the participant believes their needs cannot be met within the base budget, the policy supports this path:

1. Request the needed services anyway, even if they exceed the base budget.
2. The LME/MCO must evaluate whether the services are medically necessary.
3. If the services are found medically necessary, they are to be authorized despite the budget amount.
4. If the request is denied, the participant must receive the reason for the denial and information on how to appeal.
5. The participant may also file a grievance regarding the base budget.

## Practical takeaway

In plain language: the base budget is not supposed to operate as an absolute ceiling. A participant who needs more can ask for more, and the key question is whether the extra services are medically necessary. If the LME/MCO says no, the participant should get written reasons and appeal rights, and can also pursue a grievance about the budget.
